\chapter{The Ten Urdu Digits}
\label{ch:ur-digits}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read and write the ten Urdu digits, read a price, a bus number and a telephone number off the page, and say which way a number runs inside a right-to-left line.}

Ten signs across four lessons, grouped by what makes each set hard: the reversed direction, the one-tooth pair, the three shapes Arabic draws differently, and the mirror pair.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sifr ek]{\ur{۰} \ur{۱} — two digits, and a direction that reverses}

\label{lesson:UR-W31-digits-zero-one}



\begin{quote}
Which way does an Urdu line run? Count aloud to ten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes, and the direction}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{۰}} — \emph{sifr}, zero  \textbf{\ur{۱}} — \emph{ek}, one
\end{quote}

Urdu has its own ten digit signs, and a price ticket, a bus number, a page number and a telephone number in Pakistan are written in them. A reader who can say \textbf{ek} and cannot read \textbf{\ur{۱}} still cannot read a price.

\textbf{\ur{۰}} is a \textbf{dot}, not a ring. Fix that first: a European eye reads a dot as a decimal point, and Urdu's nine is the ring.

Now the part no earlier chapter of this book has had to say. \textbf{Numbers run left to right, inside a line that runs right to left.} Ten is \textbf{\ur{۱۰}} — one, then zero, in the order English uses — while the words on either side of it move the other way. The page changes direction at the number and changes back after it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ur{۰}} — a dot; \textbf{\ur{۱}} — a stroke
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{۱۰}} — \emph{das}, ten, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[do tīn]{\ur{۲} \ur{۳} — one tooth apart}

\label{lesson:UR-W31-digits-two-three}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ur{۰}} and \textbf{\ur{۱}}, then read \textbf{\ur{۱۰}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{۲}} — \emph{do}, two  \textbf{\ur{۳}} — \emph{tīn}, three
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{۳}} is \textbf{\ur{۲}} with one more tooth, and that is the whole difference. It is small enough that the two have to be written as a pair rather than one at a time: say \emph{do} and \emph{tīn} aloud as the hand makes them, and the shapes stop competing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ur{۲}}, then \textbf{\ur{۳}} beside it
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{۱۲}}, \textbf{\ur{۱۳}}, \textbf{\ur{۲۳}}, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chār pānch chhe]{\ur{۴} \ur{۵} \ur{۶} — the three Urdu keeps for itself}

\label{lesson:UR-W31-digits-four-five-six}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ur{۲}} and \textbf{\ur{۳}}, and say which has the extra tooth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{۴}} — \emph{chār}, four  \textbf{\ur{۵}} — \emph{pānch}, five  \textbf{\ur{۶}} — \emph{chhe}, six
\end{quote}

These three are why this chapter exists as more than a list.

Urdu and Arabic share an alphabet, letter for letter, and a reader of this book has spent twenty-five chapters on that shared inheritance. \textbf{The digits are where the sharing stops.} Seven of the ten are drawn the same way in both; \textbf{\ur{۴}}, \textbf{\ur{۵}} and \textbf{\ur{۶}} are not, and Arabic writes those three with quite different shapes.

So a reader who picked the digits up from an Arabic book will misread a Pakistani price ticket at exactly these three places and nowhere else. If you drill three of the ten harder than the rest, drill these.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ur{۴}}, \textbf{\ur{۵}}, \textbf{\ur{۶}}, saying \emph{chār}, \emph{pānch}, \emph{chhe}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{۱۴}}, \textbf{\ur{۱۵}}, \textbf{\ur{۱۶}}, left to right
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāt āṭh nau]{\ur{۷} \ur{۸} \ur{۹} — a mirror pair, and the ring}

\label{lesson:UR-W31-digits-seven-eight-nine}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\ur{۴}}, \textbf{\ur{۵}}, \textbf{\ur{۶}} — the three Arabic draws differently.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shapes}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{۷}} — \emph{sāt}, seven  \textbf{\ur{۸}} — \emph{āṭh}, eight  \textbf{\ur{۹}} — \emph{nau}, nine
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{۷}} and \textbf{\ur{۸}} are mirror images of each other, one opening upward and one downward. Write them as a pair, every time, and the mirror stops being a problem — the same trick that worked on \textbf{\ur{۲}} and \textbf{\ur{۳}}.

\textbf{\ur{۹}} is a \textbf{ring} with a tail, and this is where a dot-shaped zero earns its keep. Had \textbf{\ur{۰}} been a ring too, the page would carry two rings and no way to separate them.

Ten signs, four lessons, and the set is closed.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ur{۷}} and \textbf{\ur{۸}} as a pair, then \textbf{\ur{۹}}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\ur{۰} \ur{۱} \ur{۲} \ur{۳} \ur{۴} \ur{۵} \ur{۶} \ur{۷} \ur{۸} \ur{۹}} once, slowly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/urdu.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Urdu}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — reading the figures}

\label{lesson:UR-C31-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count aloud to ten, then say which way digits run inside an Urdu line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Read all ten signs shuffled and say each as an Urdu word.
  \item Read \textbf{\ur{۱۰}}, \textbf{\ur{۲۰}} and \textbf{\ur{۱۰۰}} and say each — \emph{das}, \emph{bīs}, \emph{sau}.
  \item Hear ten amounts named and write each in Urdu figures.
  \item Write the ten signs from dictation, out of order, checking \textbf{\ur{۴}}, \textbf{\ur{۵}} and \textbf{\ur{۶}} against the models rather than against memory.
  \item Read a seven-figure telephone number aloud, one digit at a time.
\end{enumerate}

An A1 examiner asks for an age, a price and a telephone number. All three are now reachable. What is not: \textbf{\ur{۱۱}} to \textbf{\ur{۱۹}}, whose words are nine irregular forms rather than a rule, so the figure can be read and its name cannot yet be said.
